explainer.heading: What the poem says
explainer.body: In this excerpt, a brook (small stream) speaks. It chatters as it flows to join a brimming river. It winds in and out past blossoms, trout and grayling; steals by lawns and hazel covers; slips, slides, glooms and glances; murmurs under moon and stars; lingers and loiters — and goes on forever.
explainer.example: Refrain: “For men may come and men may go, / But I go on forever.”
explainer.hook: Man is mortal; nature is eternal.

explainer.heading: Personification & imagery
explainer.body: The brook is given human actions: it chatters, steals, slides, murmurs, lingers and loiters. Images: blossoms sailing on it, trout and grayling (fish), forget-me-nots, swallows skimming the water, “netted sunbeams” dancing on sandy shallows.
explainer.example: trout, grayling = fish; cresses = water plants; shingly bars = pebbly banks.

explainer.heading: Sound words
explainer.body: Chatter, murmur — the brook’s sounds. Alliteration: “slip, I slide”, “gloom, I glance”, “sandy shallows”.

explainer.heading: Refrain
explainer.body: A refrain is a line repeated within a poem. It adds a musical, lyrical quality and highlights the theme. Here it stresses the immortality of nature against the mortality of human beings. A refrain can have small changes and can be used like a chant.

explainer.heading: The poet
explainer.body: Alfred Lord Tennyson was a leading poet of the Victorian Age (19th century) in England and Poet Laureate during Queen Victoria’s reign. Famous poems: “Break, Break, Break”, “The Charge of the Light Brigade”, “Crossing the Bar”.

questions.q: What is a refrain? Quote the refrain from “The Brook”.
questions.model: A refrain is a line or phrase repeated in a poem. In “The Brook” it is: “For men may come and men may go, / But I go on forever.”

questions.q: How does the poet convey the sense of immortality of the brook? Give examples.
questions.model: The brook speaks of its endless journey to join the river. It describes flowing past blossoms, fish, lawns and hazel covers, moving day and night “under moon and stars”, lingering and loitering. The refrain “For men may come and men may go, / But I go on forever” contrasts short human lives with the brook’s endless flow. Repetition and personification make it seem alive and eternal.
points: Flows past many places, day and night
Refrain contrasts mortal men with eternal brook
